title: The AI Notetaker Has Been Invited to All the Meetings
gist: Voice-dictation startup Wispr Flow is launching Notetaker, a meeting-transcription and chatbot-query tool, entering a crowded field already led by Granola AI and Otter AI; CEO Tanay Kothari frames 2026 as 'the year of meeting recorders and notetakers,' with most Silicon Valley conversations now assumed to be AI-recorded, often without explicit consent, despite consent laws in jurisdictions like California.

themes.theme: Meeting-recorder category is consolidating and normalizing

insights.claim: Wispr Flow CEO Tanay Kothari describes 2026 as 'the year of meeting recorders and notetakers,' and the article's author notes it's hard to argue with that in Silicon Valley, where most tech investors and other people now assume a business conversation is being recorded or transcribed by AI, sometimes without explicit consent.
insights.speaker: Tanay Kothari (via Reece Rogers)
insights.so_what: AI meeting transcription is becoming default infrastructure for professional conversations in tech circles, implying strong sustained demand for this product category and normalizing a practice with real consent/legal exposure.
insights.quote: This is the year of meeting recorders and notetakers.
insights.locator: This is the year of meeting recorders and notetakers

insights.claim: The current default option for meeting records is Granola AI, with other established players including Otter AI, into which market Wispr Flow — previously known for voice dictation — is now expanding with its new Notetaker feature.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Identifies the current competitive set (Granola AI as incumbent leader, Otter AI, and now Wispr Flow) in the AI meeting-notetaker space, useful for mapping the competitive landscape in this sub-vertical of applied AI.
insights.locator: The current option du jour for meeting records is Granola AI

insights.claim: Wispr's Notetaker connects to the user's calendar, listens during meetings, generates a post-meeting AI summary, and includes a chatbot-style tool for asking follow-up questions about the meeting's content; it launches first on Mac, with a Windows version planned later.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: The chatbot 'ask anything' query layer on top of the transcript is the differentiated feature the reviewer found most useful, suggesting retrieval/QA-over-transcript functionality is becoming a baseline expectation in this category, not just raw transcription.
insights.locator: Wispr's Notetaker connects to your calendar

insights.claim: Wispr previously capped recordings at six minutes, causing users to repeatedly start and stop the tool to cover a 30-minute meeting; the company has now removed that friction and extended the maximum recording length to six hours.
insights.speaker: Tanay Kothari (via Reece Rogers)
insights.so_what: A direct example of a startup removing an artificial usage constraint based on observed user workaround behavior — a product lesson generalizable to other session-length-limited AI tools.
insights.quote: Wispr had a six-minute time limit earlier. People would start it on and off five times just to capture a 30-minute meeting. We realized we should stop being stupid. This is what people really want Wispr to do.
insights.locator: Wispr had a six-minute time limit earlier

themes.theme: Consent and trust risk in AI transcription

insights.claim: Kothari says users should never secretly use Wispr's Notetaker and should always disclose when it's transcribing a conversation, both for legal reasons and to preserve trust, noting that recording consent laws vary by jurisdiction between single-party and multi-party consent regimes.
insights.speaker: Tanay Kothari (via Reece Rogers)
insights.so_what: Legal consent requirements (particularly in two-party consent states/jurisdictions) remain a compliance risk for meeting-transcription tools as adoption scales, and vendors are proactively pushing disclosure norms to manage that liability.
insights.quote: We need that to become the norm for everybody. Otherwise, you're going to get a lot of lack of trust that starts to happen.
insights.locator: There are laws that are single-party and multi-party

insights.claim: In San Francisco, where Wispr is based, recording a private conversation legally requires consent from all participants (two-party/multi-party consent), a jurisdiction-specific legal constraint on how the tool can be used even in its home city.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Establishes a concrete legal baseline (California two-party consent) that meeting-recording AI tools must navigate, relevant to compliance and liability assessment for the whole notetaker product category.
insights.locator: In San Francisco, where Wispr is based
